page: UpCloud STARTER-2xCPU-16GB is a starter-class virtual server configured with 2 shared vCPUs and 16.0 GB of system memory, yielding 8.0 GB of RAM per core. Built on the x86_64 architecture, it utilizes an AMD EPYC 9575F processor running at 2.0 GHz with a 16 MB L3 cache. The server includes 50 GB of local SSD storage, a single complimentary public IPv4 address, and operates under the KVM hypervisor.

Benchmark data reveals a stark contrast between single-threaded and multi-threaded capabilities. The server achieves top-tier single-core CPU performance in stress-ng and single-threaded gzip compression. However, due to its shared CPU allocation and 2-core limit, multi-threaded performance is constrained. Multi-threaded bzip3 decompression, PassMark CPU score, and database operations fall into the lower performance tiers. Memory bandwidth remains average, with read-only large block speeds at 68.93 GB/sec.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, this instance provides a high memory-to-vCPU ratio within a budget-friendly shared-resource tier, making it a viable option for memory-intensive but compute-light workloads. It is well-suited for static web serving, lightweight background processing, and small-scale application hosting. It is less suitable for heavy database operations, multi-threaded mathematical simulations, or medium-to-large language model inference due to its shared CPU allocation and weak multi-core benchmark results.
description: The UpCloud STARTER-2xCPU-16GB is an x86_64 virtual server featuring 2 shared AMD EPYC 9575F vCPUs, 16.0 GB of RAM, and 50 GB of local SSD storage. Operating under the KVM hypervisor, this instance delivers top-tier single-core CPU performance, as evidenced by its stress-ng single-core score of 3703.78 and high single-threaded compression speeds. However, its shared CPU allocation limits multi-threaded efficiency, resulting in lower-tier PassMark CPU and database benchmark scores. With a high memory-to-vCPU ratio of 8.0 GB per core, this server offers a cost-effective profile for memory-reliant workloads that do not require sustained, dedicated multi-core processing. It is best suited for static web serving, basic application hosting, and lightweight single-threaded tasks.
